title: HowTo: Identification of system-relevant packaging materials - Das neue Verpackungsgesetz (VerpackG) 2025
content:
The German “Verpackungsgesetz” basically discriminates between system-relevant and not system-relevant packaging materials:

How can you correctly differentiate between system-relevant and not system-relevant packaging? The complex definition of the “Verpackungsgesetz” is not very helpful here:

§ 3 (8) & (11) “VerpackG”: System-relevant packaging consists of sales and outer packaging filled with goods, which typically arise as packaging waste at the private consumer. Private consumers are private households and points of origin with packaging waste similar to private households. Similar points of origin are above all restaurants, hotels, roadhouses, canteens, administrative offices, barracks, hospitals, schools, welfare organisations, freelancer offices, typical points of origin in the cultural sector such as cinemas, operas, and museums as well as holiday parks, theme parks, and sport stadiums. Furthermore, similar points of origin are farms and craft businesses where paper, cardboard, plastic, metal, and composite packaging waste can be collected via usual household bins (max. 1100 liter containers per collection group) and using the regular household pickup cycle.

The misinterpretation of this definition often results in the following wrong assumptions:

Below we describe a procedure for the efficient and at the same time plausible assessment of the packaging types and weights which pass through your company and leave it onto the German market:

To determine the materials and volumes of system-relevant packaging in your company which you’d have to register, license, and report as the producer along the terms of the German “Verpackungsgesetz” you can follow the step-by-step procedure as described below:

If you’ll still not be able to finally decide about the system-relevance of your packaging after completing the procedure, you can apply for an official statement at the official German Clearing House ZSVR (“Verpackungsregister”). Currently, the application procedure is free, but, however, comes with a certain amount of bureaucracy and waiting time. You can find further details regarding the application procedure and the corresponding form on the website of the Stiftung ZSVR (regretfully only available in German language).

Otherwise, the desired amounts and material fractions of system-relevant packaging remain after completing the procedure described above.

Packaging volumes which aren’t put on the German market for the first time by your company, but by your suppliers (so-called upstream distributors) will usually have to be assessed and (if system-relevant) be registered and licensed. However, there are some exceptions:

If your company is established in Germany, you can assume and require that German suppliers either themselves or by their upstream distributors comply with the German packaging regulations, i.e. that the packaging materials have been assessed and (if system-relevant) registered and licensed. You could omit these volumes in this case.

Generally, please always check each supplier from two angles:

If both perspectives show evidence that the delivered packaging materials have already been correctly assessed and (if system-relevant) registered, you can omit these volumes.

Along the definitions of the German “Verpackungsgesetz” so called service packaging is used to enable and facilitate the handover of goods to consumers, usually at a point-of-sale, e.g. shops, snack bars, restaurants, butchers, or bakeries. Some examples of typical service packaging:

Such service packaging will always be system-relevant, and if you’re the one filling it with goods (e.g. food or beverages) at the point-of-sale, you’ll also be regarded the producer. However, along § 7 (2) “VerpackG” you can require your upstream supplier of the respective empty service packaging to cover registration and licensing along the German packaging legislation (only for future volumes, by the way), and you can omit the respective volumes. Please note that your supplier can still charge you for these extra efforts!

The German Packaging Clearing House (ZSVR) publishes a (German) catalogue of over 400 product groups which should aid producers during their decision whether or not a packaging is regarded system-relevant, or not. You can check this catalogue for your own products or product groups. You can also compare with similar product groups, if you can’t find your specific articles. However, especially for non-food products, you will often not find an entry in the catalogue. Next to the following deductions for specific packaging types, you could still apply for a binding assessment at the Clearing House or the self-assessment.

The German “Verpackungsgesetz” defines several specific packaging types which generally don’t qualify as system-relevant, and thus, won’t have to be registered or licensed:

Transport packaging (§ 3 (1) Nr. 3 “VerpackG”)

Transport packaging should “facilitate the handling and the transport of goods in a way that any contact to them as well as any damages should be avoided”. They differ from system-relevant distribution packaging by the fact that they typically never reach (private or commercial) end users. Thus, they’re always used between storages and warehouses of commercial players. These volumes can be deducted from the amounts of system-relevant packaging.

Please note that the following settings justify the classification of transport packaging as system-relevant:

Sales and outer packaging (B2B) (§ 15 (1) Nr. 2 “VerpackG”)

If packaging materials typically don’t arise as waste at private consumers and similar points of origin they’ll usually qualify as not system-relevant, and can thus be omitted during registration, licensing, and reporting. Please be careful while discriminating such fractions! Please keep in mind that the distribution channel as well as the client structure are mostly irrelevant for the classification of packaging as “B2B”. If the packed goods aren’t obviously for exclusive industrial use and the above mentioned catalogue of system-relevant products doesn’t yield any specific decision you can only apply at the German packaging Clearing House for a final assessment of your packaging fractions.

System incompatible packaging (§ 7 (5) “VerpackG”)

The German “Verpackungsgesetz” describes an exemption for packaging materials which would “substantially interfere with the handling of the proper and harmless recycling” or “endanger the public wellbeing, above all the health”. Please note that the incompatibility of such packaging materials needs to be formally assessed by the German Packaging Clearing House.

Packaging of hazardous goods (§ 12 (4) and appendix 2 “VerpackG”)

Sales packaging containing certain hazardous or dangerous goods are generally exempted from the system-relevance. Appendix 2 “VerpackG” defines four general groups of hazardous substances:

You can deduct those packaging volumes during the assessment of the system-relevant packaging volumes in your company.

Reusable packaging (§ 12 Nr. 1 “VerpackG”)

As long as a packaging is intended to be reused on a regular basis und this is supported by an appropriate reverse logistic as well as an incentive system (e.g. a suitable deposit), it’ll be regarded as reusable packaging which is not system-relevant. Upon request, the German Packaging Clearing House can finally decide about the character of a specific packaging as reusable, or not.

Disposable beverage packaging (§ 31 “VerpackG”)

Disposable packaging which is filled with beverages and complies with the requirements of § 31 “Verpackungsgesetz” (e.g. requirement for a deposit, collection facilities) will usually not qualify as system-relevant packaging.

Export volumes (§ 12 Nr. 3 “VerpackG”)

As the “Verpackungsgesetz” only applies for Germany, any volumes which are exported to other countries aren’t under the scope of the law and obviously won’t have to be assessed as system-relevant.

If you successfully performed the steps above, only the system-relevant packaging volumes should remain which you’d have to register, license, and report in Germany. For the licensing and the regular reporting the volumes would still have to be split up by their material fractions:
